thread.title: Larry Hungerford: Stocks plunged in October; will they rebound by the end of the year?

title: Larry Hungerford: Stocks plunged in October; will they rebound by the end of the year?
text:
Save
Four weeks ago, my column here raved about our fast-growing economy and predicted continuing good stock returns for the rest of 2018. I was half-right: Our U.S. economy grew 3.5 percent last quarter (better than the expected 3.3 percent), consumer confidence is near record highs, the unemployment rate is the lowest since 1969, and there are currently the most job openings ever at 7.14 million.
However, my optimistic forecast for higher stock prices was totally wrong! Despite all the good economic news, the S&P 500 had its worst month since 2011. It could have been so much worse, but stocks rose 3½ percent from their midday low Monday , Oct. 29 , ending the month with a strong two-day rally. Despite the end-of-month rebound, the S&P 500 lost 7 percent in October. It suffered a “correction” Monday , Oct. 29, when, at its low, it was down 11 percent from its all-time high on Sept. 20. (The Dow Jones Industrial Average, losing 5 percent last month, set its record high Oct. 3.)
Understanding market jargon when stocks decline is fairly simple if you know the definitions. A market “pullback” is a loss of 5 percent but less than 10 percent, a ”correction” is a 10 percent decline but less than 20 percent, and a feared “bear market” is a 20 percent sell-off or more.
Typically, bear markets only occur when the economy is weakening , heading toward a recession . Pullbacks and corrections often take place when the economy is strong, given market volatility. Since the market-crash bottom that occurred March 9, 2009, stock returns have more than quadrupled even though there have been six corrections (including this one) and 12 pullbacks.
Our last correction was in February — just eight months ago. Yet, despite our February and October corrections, the S&P 500 is basically even so far this year. And the outlook for the next 12 months is rosy, based on historical precedent. Since 1942, stocks have always been higher 12 months after midterm elections, averaging a terrific 15 percent return.
You may be saying by now, “All right Hungerford, quit your reassuring rhetoric and tell us what has gone wrong.” The sell-off began the first week in October when interest rates hit a seven-year high. Later in the month, President Donald Trump called The Federal Reserve’s interest rate increases “crazy,” and reports from Europe and elsewhere overseas indicted slowing economic growth.
The market had largely ignored the effects of tariffs until suddenly it didn’t. Even with a new trade agreement with Mexico and Canada, worries over the tariff standoff between China and the U.S. began to negatively affect the market. (Jim Hackett, the head of Ford Motor Co., said Sept. 26 on CNBC that tariffs would reduce Ford profits by $1 billion!)
Of course, no one really ever knows why the October downturn occurred. As one pundit explained in the Oct. 28 edition of Barron’s: “The psychology of the market is so irrational and excessive in its swings.” (Barron’s, 10/29/18, p. 28)
Typically, the market focuses most on corporate profits. More than 75 percent of companies reported in October that they beat third-quarter profit projections — the average is 70 percent. Companies reporting earnings last month for the third-quarter have increased profits by a terrific 20 percent year-over-year average, down only slightly from the awesome 25 percent average for 2018’s first six months.
But instead of emphasizing the bottom-line profit increases, market psychology became obsessed with top-line revenue numbers and future company growth outlooks. Amazon (AMZN) , my favorite stock and largest holding, provides a perfect example.
Despite all-time record third-quarter profits of $5.75 a share, beating its predicted $3.14 number by 83 percent, Amazon shares immediately went down 10 percent after its report. Why? It barely missed its revenue forecast on sales of $56.6 billion, compared with the expected $57.1 billion. Yet its sales were 29 percent higher than last year’s third quarter.
The real disappointment came when it provided fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $66.5 billion to $72.5 billion, below consensus estimates of $73.8 billion. Amazon also noted that its recent minimum wage increase to $15 an hour for its 470,000 employees lowered its estimate for operating income this quarter.
As the market sell-off continued, Amazon shares nose-dived. Its all-time high was $2,050 a share, set Sept. 4. It hit a low of $1,476 Tuesday morning, a discouraging 29 percent drop. It ended the month at $1,598, cratering 20 percent during October. However, even after losing a fifth of its value, it is up 37 percent so far this year. Believe it or not, Amazon has also averaged 37 percent a year since it became a public company in 1997.
I still strongly recommend Amazon; it is the leader in both cloud services and retail on-line selling where it has nearly 50 percent of all sales. (eBay is second at 6 percent.) I bought more of Amazon last month and also added to my two favorite lower-risk tech stocks, Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT). Both hit their all-time highs Oct. 3; Apple only declined 3 percent last month while Microsoft fell almost 7 percent. Both outpaced the tech-heavy NASDAQ that fell 9 percent in October, its worst monthly performance since 2009.
Last month, portfolio diversification was no help. Small-company U.S. stocks did worse than large stocks, losing 11 percent, and international stocks dropped 9 percent. Worldwide, investors lost $4.5 trillion!
The odds are that the market will rebound this month and in December, traditionally a very good month for stocks. Consumer confidence, despite the market sell-off, remains high. Christmas sales should be quite good.
Uncertainty posed by midterm elections will soon be over. Most market and political forecasters predict that the Democrats will capture the U.S. House and Republicans will continue to control the U.S. Senate. (The Democrats are defending 26 Senate seats while the GOP only has nine at risk.) If the Democrats win the Senate or gain 40 or more seats in the House — they only need 23 to gain control — , stocks could fall further.
I think the biggest threat to the market is an all-out trade-war with China if both sides, as now seems likely, begin levying job-killing 25 percent tariffs on each other’s imports starting Jan. 1.
Capital spending by businesses rose only 0.8 percent last quarter as their CEOs become more worried about the effects of tariffs.
Also, economic growth is slowing as the effects of the tax cut wear off — predictions for this quarter are less than 3 percent.
Despite the headwinds cited above, my prediction is that stock prices will be higher by the end of the year. Of course, as I have demonstrated in this column, no one ever knows when stocks will rally or fall. But let’s remember that U.S. large-company stocks have averaged 10 percent growth for both the past 30 years and since 1926.
